A cord passing around the shank of this lower motive wheel, is carried over a wheel above, carrying what may he called the escapement work of clock with a pendulum. T5y (1 10 arrival of the splendid steamship Empire City, at this port, yesterday, we received two weeks later intelligence from California and the gold diggings, being to the 15th of November. Soon after" that vessel reached her dock, we published the news in an extra; and our readers will find the whole of it in detail, as well as some interesting letters from our correspondents in that distant region, in our columns to-day. Gold dust, it appears, is as plentiful as ever in the diggings, but the rainy season had commenced, and mining operations were consequently suspended, to a great extent. A very interesting feature of the intelligence by this arrival, is the election which Look place on the tenth of November, the result of which, as far as it was ascertained at the sailing of the steamer, leaves no doubt of the ratification, by the people, of the State constitution which was formed by the convention elected for framing that instrument some time since. The democrat le party seems to he in the ascendant in California; and although it was not certain which party succeeded in electing their candidates, the probability is tii.it Peter 11. Burnett was elected by the democrats as Governor, and John Mc'Uuugal as Lieutenant Governor. It is also highly probable that the Hon: T. Butler King, of Georgia, who resigned his seat in the House of Kepresentatives a short tunc since, lor the purpose of running as Senator from Calilbrnia, w il

8 !?» OS® JZ A713. THE ORIGIN OF RILLS OF EXCHANGE. It is to the Jews that we owe the invention of bills of exchange. Often obliged to leave a country at the shortest notice, condemned by the most ferocious intolerance to a wandering life, they had invented that easy mode of taxing too highly the comforts of its carrying about their riches, as on their own people. They have intimated acexpulsion from Portugal. The invention of the bill of exchange had been fixed by some historians at that period þÿ that is, about the beginning of t lie sixteenth century ; but, there existed at V enice, in 1272, a special law upon that sort of contract. From the laborious researches of .Messrs. Blanqui and Nougier, it would appear that the exact date of this Jewish invention must reascend as far as their expulsion from France by Philip Yugustus, in 1181. Montesquieu says himself: þÿ " They had from time immemorial in their jurisprudence, models of letters of purchase, letters of donation, or letters of exchange ; these were not unlike our bills of exchange." þÿ Louis Rlanc.

A letter front I psal, of the 24th tilt., states that the Dukes of East Gotha and Dalecarlia, now students at the Eniversity of I psa!, being desirous of seeing the mortal remains of Gustavus 1. (Gustavus Vasa) which are deposited in one ot the vaults of the cathedral of that city, the marble scarcophagus containing the body was opened by virtue of a special authorisation of the king. Of the body of the great monarch nothing remains hut the skeleton ; hut all the clothes (of the ancient Spanish costume) are intact, and preserve a certain freshness. The crown, the sceptre, the globe, and the ornaments of the scabbard enclosing the royal sword, and the buckles of the girdle and shoes, arc of fine and massive gold, and partly adorned with precious stones.

Negotiations with Russia. þÿ There is no truth in the announcement made by evening paper an of the "opening of negotiations by her Majesty's representatives at St. Petersburg, with a view of increasing the commercial relations between this country and Russia." The 'commercial relations" between this country and Russia have long been on a very increased scale. In fact, it is wellknown to all persons even well-informed, that the best portion of the foreign trade of Russia has liecn carried on with England; and that the very existence of their nobles, who are all merchants, arc owing to the quantities of their produce imported into the I nited Kingdom, such as hides, tallow, hemp, and latterly corn. Some of the manufactured goods of England have been subject to a high rate of duty on their importation into Russian ports. This system has naturally operated most injuriously on the commerce of Russia, and has enhanced

the prices of these articles of necessity upon their purchasers, the subjects of the Emperor. The Russian Government, taught by example, and by the more sound and practical doctrines that have penetrated beyond Buckinghamshire, has opened its eyes on the folly of

cordingly, some time hack, their intention to modify, and to reduce, their tariff of import duties upon English goods, required for the consumption and use of their people þÿ but the opening of negotiations was not at all necessary for this purpose.

To tin: Editor or the St. Croix Avis. Sir, May I beg you will give place in your next number, to the few simple hints, which are here thrown out ; for no other purpose, but through a desire of the public good. There are at present both in the town of Christiansted and Frederiksted many handsome buildings, and many more in all probability will be added to the number in a short time, such is the enterprising spirit of the community. But I regret much to say that there are in Christiansted, and no doubt in Frederiksted also, many vacant lots open and without a fence, and that too in the most conspicuous parts of the town, which are actually a nuisance to the streets in which they are situated. In my humble opinion it is a great pity to see so many lots vacant, and the more so, because in many instances the owners are not able to have suitable houses erected on them. Would it therefore be too much to suggest that some of these lots might be purchased at the expenee of the public treasury, and dwellings erected on them, which could either he sold or leased at pleasure ; or, it this would he asking too much, at least would there he 110 possibility of allowing means from the public funds to have them properly fenced in, as also to remove certain private oIKces from within the range of the street, and thus save the passers-by as well as the neighbours at large from a most disagreeable nuisance ? In throwing out those hints, it is not my intention to impose a burden on those who hold lots of land whether va-

cant or occupied ; it is merely to suggest a propriety which must be obvious to every one, and shew that with a little system, we can very easily avoid the reproach of having one thing laughing at another. No man in his senses, would ever think of tacking an old piece of cloth on a new coat ; nor would it seem at all unworthy of those on whom the duty devolves, that while they pay attention to build up what is new, they remember to provide lor the shabby fragments of the old. To describe nil the various institutions of mercy which existed during f!ie middle ages, would he an endless task ; and to impart an adequate idea of their merits, by citing didactive pieces, v it limit, as it were, a local and minute inspection of what was established, is impossible ; for it is in such works that one perceives the truth of what an ancient French writer remarks, that the heart is more ingenious than the understanding. in cities, therefore, in deserts, amidst which cloistered brethren dwelt in happier days, wherever w e direct our steps, w ithin the realms that faith once illumined, Catholicism has left some memorial by which we know that the blessed merciful have passed, þÿ some monument, vital with mind, attesting the subtle action of a most loving heart, which, to an ordinary traveller, may seem only some nule wall, perhaps, or broken trophy, but on which a poet, with the tender penetration of a Wordsworth, may describe bis fastening " an eye tear glazed." Johnson used to say, that the real criterion of civilisation consisted in the degree of provision made for the happiness of the poor; and if that proposition be admitted, w e must conclude that the middle ages were more entitled to the praise to which the modern communities lay claim, than any other period in the history of man. To win the beatitude of the merciful, there were, it must be remembered, other virtues required in regard to the poor, besides ministering to their corporal necessities ; and truly, in fulfilling

the spiritual works of mercy towards them, the devotion of men in the middle ages was admirable, and such as can never he sufficiently praised ; hut having already had occasion to witness their employed by St. Jerome and St. Isidore. respect for the poor, their meekness in relation to them, their readiness to console, their assiduity to counsel and instruct them, it will not he necessary to give any further illustrations ; though, were time and space allowed, it would not he an unpleasant field for reminiscences. Poets, wiio sing so often the interceding grace of a St. Klino, to whose prayers the Spanish and Portuguese sailors commend their hark in tempests, w ould not he ungrateful to an historian who should remind them that this saint was known in history as St. Peter Gontpilcz, w ho had exchanged the honours and pleasures of a court for the privilege of teaching the catechism to the poor children of the fishermen and sailors on the coasts of the Peninsula. þÿ One might w rite a large book upon the education which was given to the poor, in the middle ages, by the charity of the rich. The parents of the celebrated Lewis of Grenada were indigent, obscure persons, but the marquis dc Mondejar supplied them with nicars for educating their son. Similar instances are innumerable. In the sixteenth century, in the public grammar school of Padua, founded by Annibal ilugerio, the boys arid youths of the city were taught, gratuitously, both Greek and Latin. þÿ

S T. 0 3i 0 3 X 47J3, But there yet remains unnoticed an order of facts more striking still, as attesting the passage of the blessed merciful upon earth, to examination of which we must now proceed. If we open the annals of any city, and examine the rise and progress of its charitable foundations, we cannot but feel surprise and admiration at the prodigious and persevering activity of the principle which has produced such effects. What a series of institutions, directed to some purpose of love and mercy, is presented in the history of Paris alone; and what a multitude of all ranks and estates of men co-operated with one heart and mind to conceive, establish, and perpetuate them! Kings and queens, princes, nobles, bishops, priests, magistrates; citizens, tradesmen, and even mendicants, all conspired in the same direction, and with such comprehensive and subtle skill, that no kind of misery was forgotten, or left unprovided with the fitting means to remove or alleviate it. l)t- Bourgueviile, speaking of the charitable foundations ul Caen, observes, that posterity will he able easily to judge, that their predecessors were verv faithful to God, charitable to the poor, and lirm in their hope in his mercy, when it will remark the foundations which they have left to the value, every year, of three thousand li\ res. No ancient legislator ever proposed an hospital lor the poor and infirm, or an liosmcK for the stranger and destitute. When peasants or any w anderers from the country came

into Koine, it they did not leave it after the market, they had no resource but to pass the night in the arcades, and about the forum, or in the porches hefore the temples. The Greeks were ignorant even of the name of an hospital ; the word ' nosocomiuiu" was first

It is true, in the l'rytaneum at Athens there was provided subsistence for the wives and children of those who had sufiered for their country, Imt there was no asylum in sickness. The infirm and sick are wholly overlooked in the institutions of Lycurgus, as in those of all other legislators of Greece, although the father of medicine, Hippocrates, with a solemn oath, swears, that he will visit, all his life, the poor gratuitously. In ancient Home, there was the same neglect and indillerence in regard to the poor.

The history ot the rise and progress of hospitals can be traced in few words. In the year 380, the first hospital in the west w as founded by Fabiola, a devout Human lady, w ithout the w alls of Home. St. Jerome says expressly, that "this was the first of all and lie adds, that " it was a country house, destined to receive the sick and infirm, who before used to lie stretched on the public ways." The pilgrims' hospital at Koine, built by Famniachins, became also celebrated, in 330, the priest Zotielius, who had followed Gonstantine to Byzantium, established in that city, under his protection, an hospice for strangers and pilgrims. This house was built on the plan of the

hospice at Jerusalem, w hich llircan had erected there one hundred and fifty years before Christ, in expiation for having opened and plundered the tomb of David, and in order to convert the riches, he had found there to a benevolent purpose : but it is supposed by Mongez, that this liosncE was only opened during the least of the passovcr. St. Isidore says, in his Etymologies, that " this was the first hospice for strangers." St. Basil, who founded the first hospitals of Asa, mentions a house for the reception of the sick and of travellers, built on a spot formerly uninhabited, near the city of Ca-sarea, which became afterwards the ornament of the country, and like a second citv. St. Basil used frequently to visit it, in order to instruct and console the poor. St. Chrysostoni built several hospitals at Constantinople. Justinian, in the year 350, erected, at Jerusalem, the famous hospital of St. John, and bis example was followed by iiis successors, with such zeal, that according to Dueange, in his commentary on the Byzantine History, there were thirty-five establishments of charity in that city alone; there was the iNosoeomiuni. or asylum for the sick ; the Xenodochiuni, for pilgrims and strangers; the Ptochium. or iiosrif i; for the poor ; the house of education for poor children ; the house lor orphans ; the asylum for the aged ; the Paudochiuin, or gratuitous inn ; and the house lor lunatics. SUIT S 'X. The following beautiful lines, written by bishop lluuun, were addressed to his wife whilst he was tnaking mi Episcopal visit to his immense diocese in the East Indies. To our minds, this little sonnet is inferior to none of the bishop's works, not even to his Palestine.
if ihou wert by my side, my love ! How fast would evening fail In green Bengala's palmy grove, Listening to the nightingale !
If thou, my love ! wert by my side, My babies at my knee, How gaily would our pinnace glide O'er Gunga's mimic sea I
1 miss thee at the dawning grey When, on our deck reclined, In careless ease my limbs 1 lay, And woo the cooler wind.
I miss thee when by Gunga's stream My twilight steps 1 guide, But most beneath the lamp's galo beam, I miss lltee from my side.
I spread my books, my pencil try, The lingering noon to cheer, But miss thy kind approving eye; Thy meek attentive ear.
But when of morn and eve the star Beholds me on my knee, I feel, though thou art distant far, Thy prayers ascend lor me.
Then on! then on! where duty leads, My course be onward still, O'er broad llindosian's sultry meads, O'er bleak Almorah's lull
That course, nor Delhi's kingly gates, Nor wild Malwah detain, Fur sweet the bliss us both awaits, By yonder western main.
Thv towers, Bombav. gleam bright they say, Across the dark bine sea, But ne'er were heaits so light and gayV As then shall meet in thee !

Live it ye can, is the Law of Nature ; it is, therefore, the primary duly ol till to be industrious, and in some way, contribute to the common stock of provisions, necessaries, or enjoyments. Neither nature, nor the animal economy, nor the social relations give countenance to idleness or inutility; anil those are to he regarded as base and contemptible, who live only for the sake of living, or who, by some cralt, or some abuse of institutions, seek to live bv the industry of others. Those who produce nothing, and who contribute nothing either for their own support, or the support and enjoyment of others, are, in every community, a public nuisance. The poor, under the Mosaic law, were entitled to the tithe of every third year; to one-sixtieth of the crops every year; and to full half of every seventh year. Every great branch of trade might he made to provide for its own sick, crippled, and aged members, by weekly con-

An industrious operative, or ingenious mechanic, is entitled, in old age, to at least as much public gratitude as a sol- i scholar, artist, physician, player, or bufd ier or a sailor. The poor, in general, consider a workhouse and a prison as synonymous. þÿ Poverty, therefore, begets desperation ; and desperation crime. That kind of fund by which every trade might support its own indigent and aged members, has lately been established among the London booksellers. The arrangements have been carefully made, and, in working, we trust it will meet, in a fraternal spirit, the necessities of men who have devoted their skill to the lottery of books, and their lives as honest assistants, so that the trade may rise to the moral estimate of society. In all questions about the poor, it should be considered that law-makers and governors are of the class of the rich; and that, to improve the condition of poverty, concessions and sacrifices are demanded of the rich. The most that the laws of wealthy legislators attempt, is to vary the relations of poverty anil industry; and, it is forgotten, that of nothing, nothing ean come. In British society, i)-!()ths of the property is di\ ideil among l-10th of the people, or, in other words, only l-10th of the property is divided among U-lOths ; and,

it is the unwearied study of the rich law-makers and the 10th to protect their own rights, whatever may be the consequence to the 9-10ths. Wealth and poverty, in a community, arc more relations of the common stock of property. When a man gets rich, he abstracts from his neighbours ; and, when others become poor, their property has, by some means, passed to others. If a merchant imports, he uses his trade only as a means of personal accumuhilion. If he increase the public stock of 1000 to 1001. he merely reduces the relative value of every portion. livery wise and just king should, as his primary duty, be the king and protector of the poor, and leave the nobility and wealthy to their own power to protect themselves. Kings ought to know that they are tiie ualancio-siieet between wealth and poverty ; and no king, worthy of his office, ought ever to sanction laws made bv aristocratic legislators to rob and oppress the poor. It is with the poor-laws as with other laws, they must be just and liberal to be respected and become operative. Harsh and cruel laws are always defeated by the moral sense and christian charity of the community. A reckless and insulted poor w ill not he managed with less cxpencc than a grateful poor. Virtue and industry ought to lie singled out, promoted, and specially honoured by formal institutions ; while vice and incorrigible crime should be J subject to ignominious punishments. þÿ Youth should he usefully educated and trained to some employment, and virtuous old age he honourably provided for. þÿ It. Pi ties or ax Indian Officer. þÿ In his address to the students at Addis eomhe, .Sir Andrew Galloway thus concludes: þÿ Of you, gentlemen, who have finished your course of study, I cannot lake leave without offering you a few words of counsel. You have hitherto been under the care of others þÿ you are now to he left to yourselves. Yon are to join the Indian army. The achievements of that army, within a period of amazing briefness, have won for the arms of England a magnificent empire. You, my young friends, now so young, will one day he the guardians of that great empire. To you, gentlemen, and to your comrades, will he committed

army, and the continuance of its renown. I low is tiiis to he obtained / 1 have told you before, and 1 tell you again, it is hy the untiring energy, the self-devotion, the daring courage of its British officers. It is by commanding the confidence, b\ winning the affections of vonr men, that you will secure the faithful energy of the native army ; and it is thus you will lead them to incessant victory. .No matter what odds, to tight has been to conquer. But, gentlemen, remember the attainments required of you before you he worthy the command of such men. They are strangers to you lti manners, in customs, and tu religion. You must acquire their language first of all. You must learn their customs. You must respect their rt ligious ceremonies. You must not only be their officer hut their friend. They will lean upon vou as such. They will tell you their wants and their grievances, and you will listen to them and procure them r; dress. You must know every man in your company, and call them all hy their names. You must he jus! and kind and patient with them, hut not familiar; and vou must exact from them freely every duty. \ ii army of irt'UCO men, hacked hy upwards of TkOiM) of the illustrious army of England, for such is the Indian army . þÿ an army so officered and so united, so discij lined and so led, can never he overthrown. V ith respect to your treatment of the people generally, let me recommend to vou the most patient forbearance. They will not willingly of-

fend you; let not therefore, any misapprehension on their part or on your ow n rutile your temper towards them. þÿ You will thus secure their respect and \iiur own comfort. I repeat what l before told you, that 1 have never know n a man habitually ill-tempered to 1 lie natives rise to eminence in the service.

English against Araiis.þÿ A match is under negotiation for a race of English horses w ith the Arab horses of the Pacha of Egypt, to he run in the desert ; and the contest excites no small interest both on the Nile and the Thames. þÿ Though only a sport, it lias some practical use. Englishmen have been so long accustomed to success in many things, that they are too ready to presume its perpetuity ; and perhaps a harmless þÿrebuff should , it he encountered, may not be unsalutarv. Our countrymen have often boasted, that for all the wild case and hardy training of the Indian, þÿ English bone and þÿmuscle, hy steam-heated surfaces ; the operaþÿ English pluck and þÿbottom, could beat him in a loot race : the mistake was exposed lately Canada, in where Englishmen and Americans were easily beaten hy an Indian runner; the winner himself having been previously beaten by fleeter Indians who ran in the same race, hut reserved themselves in case of his failure. It is the great argument in favour of horse-racing, that it keeps up and improves our breed horses. Docs it of really ? To our laic eyes, the horses of our cavalry do not look as they used in years gone bv ; those of the þÿ crack
like. The cheap and multitudinous omnilmsscs have decidedly improved the breed of horses about London: as Jl. þÿ1 iorentino says, þÿ splendid cattle now

, drag our bulky vehicles, often without need for whip ; and the cab can display a steed that would make an old hackneycoachman mistake his descendant the the cabman for a lord or a sporting gent. But we doubt whether w e are at all indebted for that improvement to the racing-stud, nor do we rest our national fame on the cab or omnibus. Is not the race-horse an abstraction/ The hunter, | indeed, must have the staple of the horse in him ; hut then Air. John Bright is going D> abolish hunting along with game. It appears likely that our English sportsmen will not risk a racer against the Arabs; he goes wonderfully, with his þÿ tremendous þÿstride, over an artificial smooth turf race-course ; but he is a carpet knight. It is the steeple chaser that will be list'll ; hut steeplechases too are going to he given up þÿ þÿ they are so þÿcruel. So that even if our most serviceable horses win they are ot a kind that is to depart from amongst us. And if they lose / Why then, we say, the lesson will not he unwholesome. Beaten on foot, and on horse-hack, we may try what we can do on the water, against some worthy competitor, before we have to do it again in the day ot mortal contest. þÿ Spectator.

Rebe, the Pole, was only 32 inches at his death, aged 23, and slender in faculties. Borulawski was only 28 inches at 22, yet a man of talents. In Yea, a man was lately living, covered from head to foot with hair. The hair on tiie face was shaggy, and about eight inches long. On the breast and shoulders it was from four to live. At Ava he married a Burmese woman, by whom he has two daughters; the eldest resembles her mother, but the youngest is covered with hair like her father. The foot of a Chinese female, from the heel to the great toe, measures only four inches; the great toe is bent abruptly backwards, and its extremity pointed directly upwards: while the phalanges of the other toes are doubled in beneath the sole of the foot, having scarcely any breadth across the foot, where it i : naturally broadest. The heel, instead of projecting backwards, descends in a straight line from the bones of the leg, and imparts a singular appearance to the foot, as if it were kept in a state of permanent extension. From the doubling in of the toes into the sole of the foot, the external edge of the foot is formed, in a great measure, by the extremities of the metatarsal bones ; and a deep cleft or hollow appears in the soles. Bachael Hertz, of Copenhagen, had, between Fcl>. 1819, and, July 1822, 395 needles extracted from tumours in all parts oi lier body ; the breasts, the naval,

the thighs, lumbar region, &c. She had for fifteen years been variously diseased, and was supposed to have swallowed the needles in tits of delirium. A female, who, in 1829, was 12 years of age, and resided at Pyriacre, near Belpli, had, from disease, not eaten any thing since 1818, nor drank any thing since 1820. Total exhaustion was prevented by damp wrappers. In 18IM) a French prisoner, at Liverpool, exhibited a most extraordinary propensity to devour nauseous diet, particularly cats, of which, in one year, he eat 174, many of them while alive. An Esquimaux boy supplied by Captain I'arry, eat in one day 10j lbs. of solid food, and drank of various liquids 1£ gallon. A man of the same nation ate 10 lbs. of solids including two candles, and drank If gallons, yet they were only from 4 to 4 leet high. A soldier of 17 named Tararc, ate 24 lhs. of leg of beef in 24 hours ; and, on another occasion, all the dinner prepared for 15. Cornaro, the dietetic, allowanced himself to 12 oz. of dry food, and 14 oz. of liquids per day, from the age of 40 to 100. Nothing can be more shocking or horrid than one of our kitchens sprinkled with Blood, and abounding with the cries of creatures expiring, or with the limbs of dead animals scattered or hung up here and there. It gives one the image of a giant's den in romance, bestrewed with scattered heads and mingled limbs. þÿ Pope. Anthropophagi, or feeders on human tlesli, have existed in all ages, and still exist in Africa, and the South Sea Islands. Diogenes asserted, that we might, as well cat the tlesh of men as the tlesh of other animals. The Greeks inform us, it was a primitive and universal custom. Some of their gods lived on human flesh, and the Cyclops did the same. Aristotle and Herodotus name various nations v.bo preferred human flesh to that of animals, Giagas, and several African nations, have the same preference ; and we remember the practices at Owyhee, New Zealand, Ac. Ac. þÿ Human tlesh has the flavour of hog's flesh, and veal. Voltaire says, that, in 1725, he saw four savages from the Mississippi, one of whom, a female, admitted that she had eaten men ; but contended that Meters ought to have the preference over w ild beasts. St. Jerome states, that he saw Scotch-

They had likewise been dril- I led into the best possible behaviour towards each other ; no snarling, harking, or indecorous conduct took place when they were assembled in company. But what was most surprising of all, they were able to perform in various theatrical pieces of the character of pantomimes, representing various transactions in heroic and familiar life with wonderful fidelity. The object of their I proprietor was, of course, to make I money by their performances, which the public were accordingly invited to witi ness in one of the minor theatres. Amongst their histrionic performances was the representation of a siege. On the rising of the curtain, there appeared three ranges of ramparts, one above the having salient angles and a moat, like a regularly-constructed fortification. In the centre of the fortress arose a tower, on which a Hag was flying; \v bile in the distance behind appeared the buildings and steeples of a town. The ramparts were guarded by soldiers in uniform, each armed with a musket or sword, of an appropriate size. All these were dogs, and their duty was to defend the walls from an attacking party, consisting also of dogs, whose movements | now commenced the operations of the siege. In the foreground of the stage ! were some rude buildings and irregular i surfaces, from among which there issued a reconnoitring party ; the chief, habited as an ofliccr of rank, with great circumspection surveyed the fortification ; and

Iris sedate movements, and his consultations with the troops that accompanied bleed þÿ him, implied than an attack was determined upon. But these consultations did not pass unobserved by the defenders ot tiie garrison. The party was noticed hy sentinel, and fired upon ; a and this seemed to be the signal to call every man to his post at the embrasures. Shortly after, tiie troops advanced to the escalade; but to cross the moat, and get at the bottom of the walls, it was necessary to bring up some species of ponton, and accordingly several soldiers w ere seen engaged in pushing before them wicker-work scaffoldings, which moved on castors towards the fortifications. The drums beat to arms, and the fearful bustle of warfare opened in earnest. Smoke was poured out in volleys from shot-holes ; the besieging forces pushed forward in masses, regardless of the lire ; the moat was filled with the crowd ; and, amid much confusion and scrambling, scaling-ladders were raised against the walls. Then was the grand tug of war. The leaders of the forlorn-hope who first ascended, were opposed with great gallantry by the defenders ; and this was perhaps the most interesting part of the exhibition. þÿ The chief of the assailants did wonders ; he was seen now here, now there, animating his men, and was twice hurled, w ith ladder and followers, from the secprietor had bestowed an immense deal ond gradation of ramparts ; hut lie was invulnerable, and seemed to receive an they had been taught to walk on their accession of courage on every fresh re-

nature. The rattle of the miniature cannon, the roll of the drums, the sound of trumpets, and the heroism of the actors on both sides, imparted an idea of reality that for the moment made the spectator forget that he was looking on a performance of dogs. Not a bark was heard in the stru c irol0. o Alter numerous hairbreadth escapes, the chief surmounted the third line of fortifications, followed by his troops; Ihe enemy's standard was hurled down, and the British flag hoisted in its place; the ramparts were manned by the conquerors; and the smoke cleared awav þÿ to the tune of " God Save the King."
